extract:
Sattal or Sat Tal (lit. 'Seven lakes') is an interconnected group of seven freshwater lakes situated in the Lower Himalayan Range near Bhimtal, a town of the Nainital district in Uttarakhand, India. During the British Raj, the area had a tea plantation, one of four in the Kumaon area at that time.
The lakes sit at an altitude of 1370 metres below lush orchards in the Mehragaon valley.
Set amongst dense forests of oak and pine trees, Sattal is one of the few unspoiled and unpolluted freshwater biomes in India. These lakes are a paradise for migratory birds. It is home to a few camps being operated mostly by local people catering to tourists looking for outdoor vacations.


Geology and physiography
Sattal is situated in the Lower Himalayan Range and is the result of tectonic activities and the uplifting of sediments between the Tibetan plain and the Indo-Gangetic plains. The rocks are mainly sedimentary rocks and quartzite. Physiographically the area can be divided into lower Himalayas and terraces.


Ecology
Sattal is an ecologically fragile mesotrophic group of lakes and under the impact of heavy environmental degradation. Extensive deforestation, dumping of non-biodegradable waste, uncontrolled urbanization of the catchments and nearby forest is harming the ecology of the area. This results in scanty rainfall, a decrease in the number of plant and animal species and rapid drying up of perennial springs. The lakes also suffer from a reduced oxygen content and high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus. Poaching has eliminated many wild animals. Khudariya Tal became Sukha Tal (Dry Lake) due to the leakage of water from its western extremity. An extensive growth of invasive plants such as Lantana, Parthenium and Eichhornia is also endangering the ecological survival of the lakes.


Flora and fauna


Biological diversity
Sattal is unique for its biodiversity and ecological amplitude. It is known to be a birding paradise and supports a number of local and migratory birdlife. It has 500 species of resident and migratory birds, 20 species of mammals, over 525 species of butterflies and over 11,000 species of moths, beetles, bugs and other insects. The flora covers a wide and diverse range of plants ranging from Bryophytes, orchids, rare climbing plants, ferns, lichens, fungi, medicinal herbs and shrubs. Each individual lake has its own unique Diatom index. The Trophic Diatom Index uses the composition of freshwater diatom assemblages to assess water quality and ecological status.


Birds
 
 
The unique avian fauna of Sattal includes red-billed blue magpie, kingfishers, blue-throated and brown-headed barbets, lineated barbet, golden-throated barbet, great barbet, coppersmith barbet plum-headed parakeet, slaty-headed parakeet, chestnut bellied rock thrush, tits, babblers, jungle owlet, pied woodpecker, brown-capped pygmy woodpecker, grey-capped pygmy woodpecker, brown-fronted woodpecker, stripe-breasted woodpecker, yellow-crowned woodpecker, rufous-bellied woodpecker, crimson-breasted woodpecker, Himalayan woodpecker, lesser yellownape woodpecker, greater yellow-naped woodpecker, streak-throated woodpecker, grey-headed woodpecker, scaly-bellied woodpecker, common flameback woodpecker, Indian tree pies, blue whistling-thrush, lammergeier, Himalayan griffon, crested serpent eagle, flycatchers, Kalij pheasant, dollarbird, leaf birds, flowerpecker, purple sunbird, brown headed stork-billed kingfisher, stork-billed kingfisher, crested kingfisher, white-throated kingfisher, pied kingfisher, common kingfisher, blue-eared kingfisher, Himalayan kingfisher, Mrs. Gould's sunbird, green-tailed sunbird, black-throated sunbird, black-breasted sunbird, crimson sunbird, fire-tailed sunbird, thick-billed flowerpecker, plain-leaf flowerpecker, fire-breasted flowerpecker, russet sparrow,black-headed jay, scaly-breasted cupwing, black-capped sibia, blue whistling thrush, finches, mountain hawk eagle, black eagle, Eurasian jay, white-rumped needletail, black-headed jay, black-lored, black-throated tits, black bulbul, ashy-throated warblers, black-chinned babbler, rufous-breasted accentor, red-billed blue magpie, grey-winged blackbird, Eurasian griffon, common buzzard, black-chinned babbler, pink-browed rosefinch, common wood pigeon (Columba palumbus), slaty-headed parakeet (Psittacula himalayana), laughingthrush (Garrulax leucolophus), chestnut-tailed minla (Actinodura strigula), lemon-rumped warblers (Phylloscopus chloronotus), and many more.


Fish
Sattal has many different varieties of fish. Mahseers (Tor tor and Tor putitora) are found here in large numbers. Labeo rohita, Cirrhinus mrigala, Schizothorax richardsonii and Catla catla are some of the other fish found in the lakes.


Butterflies and moths

Some of the butterflies found at Sattal includes Indian Fritillary (Argynnis hyperbius), Peacock Pansy (Junonia almana), Blue Peacock (Papilio arcturus), Paris Peacock (Papilio paris), Red-base Jazebel (Delias pasithoe), Red lacewing (Cethosia biblis), Yellow Pansy (Junonia hierta), Tawny Rajah (Charaxes bernardus), Red Helen (Papilio helenus), Large silverstripe (Argynnis childreni), Indian oakleaf (Kallima inachus) and thousands of others. The forests also homes one of the largest moth in the world, the Atlas moth (Attacus atlas) . The Atlas moth is one of the largest lepidopterans, with a wingspan measuring up to 24 cm (9.4 in) and a wing surface area of about 160 cm2 (~25 in2). It is only surpassed in wingspan by the white witch (Thysania agrippina) and Attacus caesar, and in wing surface area by the Hercules moth (Coscinocera hercules). As in most Lepidoptera, females are noticeably larger and heavier than males, while males have broader antennae.


Adventure and excursions


Butterfly museum
There is a butterfly museum built by Frederic Smetacek Sr at Jones Estate, now Peter Smatacek is continuing the research, which has over 2500 butterfly and moth specimens and 1100 species of insects that are found in this region.


Sattal Mission Estate and Methodist Ashram
The Sattal Christian Ashram was established by E. Stanley Jones (1884-1973), the evangelist and missionary. This Christian Ashram is situated on the banks of Sattal lakes, on a former tea estate. St. John's Church is part of this ashram and showcases a mixed colonial architecture. There is also a Sattal Christian Ashram chapel situated nearby. It was established in 1930 to introduce Christianity into the Kumaun region of Uttarakhand.


Subhash Dhara
There is a natural spring of fresh water arising out of dense oak forest west of Sattal that leads to a waterfall beyond the Sukhatal also known as the Bharat tal.

wikivoyageExtract:
Sattal (सातताल Sāttāl) is a cluster of seven interconnected freshwater lakes in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand, India. Nestled at an altitude of 1,370 m within dense oak and pine forests, it is a tranquil haven for birdwatchers, nature lovers, and those seeking a quiet alternative to the bustling hill stations of Nainital and Bhimtal.


Understand

Sattal, literally “seven lakes,” is a unique freshwater ecosystem formed by tectonic depressions filled by monsoon runoff and underground springs. The lakes — Purna Tal, Ram Tal, Sita Tal, Laxman Tal, Nal‑Damayanti Tal, Sukh Tal, and Garud Tal — are interconnected, varying in size and character. Unlike the more tourist‑heavy Nainital, Sattal remains largely unspoiled, visited primarily by ecotourists, birders, and families wanting a peaceful retreat.
The area falls within a designated Important Bird Area (IBA) and supports over 500 bird species, both resident and migratory. The forests are rich in oak, rhododendron, and pine, sheltering butterflies, barking deer, wild boar, and an occasional leopard. A Christian ashram and mission estate, established by E. Stanley Jones in the 1930s, adds a spiritual dimension to the lakes.


Culture
Mythological origin: Locals believe the lakes were created when the Pandavas (of the Mahabharata) stayed here during their exile. The seven lakes are said to represent the seven sages (Saptarishi). Nal‑Damayanti Tal takes its name from the legendary king Nala and his queen Damayanti, whose love story is told in the Mahabharata.
Festivals: During the summer, a small mela (fair) is held at the lakeside, featuring local Kumaoni folk music (Jagar) and dance (Chholiya). The ashram organises Christmas and Easter services that draw visitors from across the region.
Art and craft: A few local women sell hand‑made woollen caps and bamboo baskets near the main gate. These are authentic Kumaoni crafts, and buying from them directly supports the community.


Climate

Best visiting season is March–May and October–November. Summers are mild and pleasant; winters are cold, with occasional frost. Monsoon (June–September) is heavy, transforming the forest into a lush paradise, though some trails become slippery and leech‑prone.


Read
Birds of the Indian Subcontinent by Richard Grimmett, Carol Inskipp, Tim Inskipp — an essential field guide for Sattal’s rich avifauna.
The Seven Lakes of Kumaon (Uttarakhand Forest Department, 2018) — a small publication detailing the ecology and legends of Sattal.
E. Stanley Jones and the Sattal Ashram (Methodist Historical Society) — chronicles the founding of the Christian ashram and its spiritual ethos.


Get in
Sattal is about 25 km from Haldwani/Kathgodam and 4 km from Bhimtal. The nearest railhead is Kathgodam Railway Station (KGM).


By road
From Haldwani/Bhimtal: Take NH‑109 to Bhimtal, then a narrow 4 km road towards Sattal. Shared jeeps ply from Bhimtal bazaar (₹20–30). Taxis charge around ₹300–400 one‑way.
From Nainital: 21 km via Bhimtal. A taxi takes about 45 min.
From Delhi: Drive via Moradabad–Rudrapur–Haldwani–Bhimtal (approx 310 km, 8 hr). At Kathgodam station, local travel agencies rent cars with drivers.


By train
1 Kathgodam Railway Station (KGM). The main railhead. From Kathgodam, taxis and shared cabs reach Sattal in about 45 min (₹600–900). Buses to Bhimtal also run from Haldwani ISBT. 


Get around

Sattal is small enough to explore on foot. The main lake, Purna Tal, has a well‑trodden path connecting the shores. To reach the other lakes, forest trails branch off from the main road. A vehicle is only needed to reach Sattal from Bhimtal. Once you're within Sattal, walking is the best way to soak in the silence.

Walking trails: Marked paths link Purna Tal to the adjacent lakes and the Christian Ashram. A popular loop passes through the oak forest behind the mission estate.
Local transport: There are no rickshaws or buses inside Sattal. Cycle on hire is available at a few guesthouses.
Boats: Paddle boats and kayaks can be rented at the main jetty (₹150–300 per hour).


See


The seven lakes & nature
1 Purna Tal (Main Lake). The largest and most accessible lake. A boating jetty, a small café, and a short walking path encircle its shore. The lake is rich in fish and attracts kingfishers, herons, and migratory ducks. 
2 Ram Tal & Sita Tal. Connected to Purna Tal by narrow channels. These smaller, shadier lakes are surrounded by thick foliage and offer secluded spots for birdwatching. Often less crowded. 
3 Laxman Tal & Nal‑Damayanti Tal (North‑western cluster, a 15‑min walk from the main lake). A tranquil pair, ideal for quiet contemplation. Nal‑Damayanti Tal is the deepest, with clear water reflecting the surrounding hills. 
4 Sukh Tal & Garud Tal (Slightly east of Purna Tal, accessible via a forest trail). Sukh Tal (“Happy Lake”) is a shallow, lily‑covered pool. Garud Tal is the smallest, often dried up by summer’s end. 


Spiritual & heritage
5 Sattal Christian Ashram (Methodist Ashram). Established in the 1930s by Dr. E. Stanley Jones, this serene estate houses a chapel, a guesthouse, and a library. The Sunday service (in English and Hindi) is open to all. The ashram’s simple stone architecture blends with the forest. 
6 St. John’s Church (Within the ashram compound). A beautiful stone church with stained‑glass windows, set amidst tall pines. The quiet churchyard is a place for meditation. 
7 Subhash Dhara (A 1‑km walk from the main road; ask for the trail behind the ashram). A natural spring emerging from the hillside, named after Subhash Chandra Bose. The water is crystal clear and considered sacred. A small temple sits beside the spring. 
8 Lakeside temples. A cluster of tiny shrines dedicated to Shiva, Hanuman, and local deities at the edge of Purna Tal. Offerings of flowers and bells ring gently in the breeze. 


Itineraries
Half‑day: Morning birding walk → Boating on Purna Tal → Visit Butterfly Museum → Light lunch at a lakeside stall.
Full day: Sunrise walk to Subhash Dhara → Explore the ashram and St. John’s Church → Afternoon hike around all seven lakes → Sunset viewpoint above Purna Tal.
Two‑day retreat: Day 1 as above; Day 2 forest trek to the Himalayan viewpoint, afternoon at leisure with a book from the ashram library, evening bonfire at a guesthouse (weather permitting).


Do


Activities
 Kayaking & boating. Kayaks and pedal boats are available for rent at the main jetty (approx ₹150–300/hr). Paddle to the quieter corners of Purna Tal, especially at sunrise when the mist rises. 
 Forest walks & trekking. A well‑known trail leads from the ashram through oak forest to a viewpoint offering a panoramic glimpse of the Himalayan peaks (on clear days). Another trail circumnavigates all seven lakes (approx 5 km, 2–3 hr). Maps are available at the forest checkpost. 
 Butterfly spotting. With over 100 recorded species, Sattal is a butterflying paradise. Post‑monsoon (September–October) is peak butterfly activity. The forest edges and stream beds are excellent spots. 
 Angling. With a permit from the Forest Department (available at the Bhimtal office), catch‑and‑release fishing for mahseer is possible in certain stretches. The season is March–June and October–November. 


Birdwatching & wildlife
 Birding trails. Sattal is one of India’s premier birding destinations. Walk the forest paths at dawn to spot red‑billed blue magpie, orange‑flanked bush robin, black‑headed jay, and migrant flycatchers. The mission estate and the ridge above Purna Tal are prime zones. Local guides (available at the forest checkpost) charge ₹500–1,000 for a morning walk. 
9 Sattal Butterfly Museum (Near the main lake entrance). A small, private collection showcasing the region’s astonishing butterfly diversity. Over 50 species are displayed; the curator can guide you to nearby hotspots. Entry ₹30. 


Buy
Sattal is not a shopping destination. There are no permanent markets; a few small stalls near the main lake sell:

Local honey — Raw, forest‑flower honey sold by villagers.
Woollen hand‑knits — Caps, scarves, and gloves made by local women’s cooperatives.
Postcards and birding guides — The Butterfly Museum and a small bookstore at the ashram stock field guides to birds and butterflies of the Kumaon region.
Basic necessities — For anything beyond snacks, Bhimtal (4 km) has pharmacies, a small market, and an ATM.
There are no ATMs in Sattal. The nearest ATM is in Bhimtal (4 km). Carry sufficient cash.


Eat
Dining in Sattal is simple and centred around family‑run eateries attached to guesthouses.

Kumaoni thali: Many guesthouses serve authentic meals with Bhatt ki Churkani, Aloo Gutke, Mandua roti, and seasonal greens. Advance ordering ensures freshly prepared food.
Cafés & dhabas: A couple of small cafés near the main lake offer tea, coffee, instant noodles, and basic sandwiches. The ashram’s guesthouse dining room serves simple vegetarian meals (guests only).
No alcohol: Sattal is a dry zone; there are no bars or wine shops. Drinking in public is strongly discouraged.


Drink
Chai: The quintessential mountain tea, available at all small stalls and dhabas (₹10–20).
Local spring water: The water from Subhash Dhara is potable; many visitors fill bottles there. Otherwise, stick to boiled or bottled water from guesthouses.
Burans squash: Occasionally available from local vendors; a refreshing rhododendron‑flower drink.


Sleep
Accommodation ranges from basic forest‑facing camps to comfortable guesthouses and the historic ashram.

Forest camps & eco‑lodges: Several operators set up Swiss tents and eco‑huts in the forest fringe, offering a rustic, close‑to‑nature experience. Campfires, guided walks, and meals are usually included (₹2,000–5,000 per night).
Family‑run guesthouses: Simple, clean rooms with attached bathrooms and hot water are available near the main lake and along the approach road. Expect quiet nights and personalised Kumaoni meals (₹800–2,000).
Sattal Christian Ashram guesthouse: A unique option: basic but peaceful rooms within the ashram estate. Guests can join morning prayers and meals. Book in advance directly through the ashram.
No luxury hotels: Sattal’s charm lies in its simplicity; those seeking resorts should stay in Bhimtal or Nainital.


Emergency contacts


Stay safe
Monsoon hazards: Trails can be slippery; leeches are common in dense undergrowth. Use salt or repellent. Avoid isolated areas during heavy rain.
Narrow roads: The road from Bhimtal is narrow with sharp bends. Drive carefully; parking near the main lake is limited.
Wildlife: Monkeys are bold — secure food and don’t feed them. Leopards are occasionally spotted at dusk; avoid solitary walks after dark.
Water safety: Swimmming is not allowed in the lakes. Boating is generally safe, but life jackets are limited; insist on one.


Stay healthy
The nearest hospital is in Bhimtal (4 km). Carry basic first‑aid; pharmacies are only in Bhimtal.


Respect
Remove shoes at the small lakeside temples; modest dress is appreciated.


Connect
Mobile networks are weak in many lakeside areas; Airtel and Jio work best. Guesthouses usually have Wi‑Fi, but speeds are slow. The nearest post office is in Bhimtal (PIN 263136). Internet cafés do not exist; plan to disconnect and unwind.


Go next
All destinations are connected by shared jeeps and taxis from Bhimtal.
